en: *The Treatise on the Non-Conceptual Nature of Bodhicitta*,
composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Translated by the Dharma-transmitting Master, the Purple-robed Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree. I take refuge in all Buddhas!
I shall now briefly explain the meaning of bodhicitta.
With the utmost sincerity, I prostrate to that bodhicitta; its significance is just like that of a valiant army wielding superior weapons.

As for that great bodhicitta, it is because all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have arisen from the generation of this bodhicitta that my own generation of bodhicitta is likewise accomplished; until I sit at the site of enlightenment and attain the fruit of perfect awakening, this mind shall remain firm and steadfast.
Furthermore, this bodhicitta is the gate of practice for the dhāraṇīs of all bodhisattvas; it is to be contemplated in this way and generated in this way.

I now praise and expound upon bodhicitta in order to cause all sentient beings to cease the suffering of saṃsāra, so that those not yet crossed over may all be enabled to cross over, those not yet liberated may attain liberation, those not yet at peace may attain peace, and those not yet in nirvāṇa may attain nirvāṇa.

In order to fulfill such a supreme vow, to establish the correct nature of its own characteristic as the cause, and to enter into the contemplation of ultimate reality, this unarisen self-characteristic of that bodhicitta is now explained.
That which is called bodhicitta is free from all natures. Question:
In this context, how is it free from all natures?

Answer: It refers to the aggregates, bases, and elements being free from all grasping and rejection; the equality of the selflessness of phenomena; and the fact that one’s own mind is fundamentally unarisen because its intrinsic nature is empty.
Within this context, what is meant by "self"?

Although the aggregates and so forth are manifest and discerned, the discriminating mind that appears before them has no intrinsic reality; therefore, if one constantly awakens to and realizes the bodhicitta, one will be able to abide in the empty nature of all phenomena.

Furthermore, one constantly awakens to that bodhicitta, which, when observed with a compassionate mind, has great compassion as its essence; because it is thus, no mark of a self can be found within the aggregates.
There are certain non-Buddhists who engage in inappropriate practices and cling to conceptual distinctions, asserting that the aggregates exist and are not impermanent phenomena.

In reality, however, the characteristics of "self" and "other" cannot be apprehended; within the true nature that sustains all phenomena, one cannot grasp them as either permanent or impermanent. Since even the name "self" has no reality within the aggregates, how much less could there be any agency or conceptual constructions?
If one says that there is a single dharma, or even that there are various dharmas, such a speaker turns their mind toward the world and follows worldly conduct.
That is not appropriate, for it constitutes the characteristic of eternalism.
This interpretation is incorrect; therefore, one should know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, and whether internal or external, they cannot be differentiated.
What cause could there be for that grasping mind such that it cannot transcend the characteristics of worldly convention?
If the cause and the characteristic are non-dual, then this is neither impermanent nor a grasper.
One should know that the nature of the mind cannot be grasped as permanent; therefore, its impermanence is itself permanence.
If one knows that their nature is impermanent, what should be done, and from what could one give rise to the perception of a self?

If one is detached from the world, there will be no obstruction within the aggregates; likewise, regarding the spheres or elements, such realization is also the case, and the two dharmas of grasping and abandoning cannot be found.

Regarding the term "aggregates" (*skandha*) used herein, it refers to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; these are called the five aggregates, and the śrāvakas train therein.

Furthermore, it should be understood that form is like a mass of foam, sensation is like a bubble, perception is like a mirage, mental formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is like a magical illusion.
Regarding the meaning of these five aggregates, the Buddha, the Honored One among two-legged beings, has taught them as appropriate for all bodhisattvas.

As for what is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), I shall now briefly indicate its characteristics: the four great elements and that which is derived from them are designated as the aggregate of form.
That which is not form refers to the remaining three aggregates: feeling, perception, and formations.
One should know from various teachings that these constitute the aggregate of formations; perception will be explained below as it follows.
Herein, "bases" (āyatana) refers to the internal bases such as the eye and the external bases such as visible form; these are spoken of as the twelve bases.

In this context, "elements" (dhātu) refers to the elements of the eye-faculty and so forth, the elements of eye-consciousness and so forth, and the objective spheres of form and so forth; these are designated as the eighteen elements.

Thus, the aggregates, bases, and elements are free from all grasping or rejecting; they have no spatial location, no divisions, and cannot be conceptually differentiated. It is not correct for one who views them through conceptual differentiation to do so, for as soon as conceptual differentiation arises, there is attachment.
Furthermore, how is this brought into correspondence?
If there were a single characteristic that perceived external objects, one should know that this is overturned by the wisdom of deconstruction.
What is the meaning of "the mind nourishing form"?
One should understand that they are thus neither identical nor different.
There are certain non-Buddhists, such as the Pāramārthikas and others, who give rise to threefold conceptualization according to their various divergent views.
This interpretation is not correct. For example, when a person commits an act of killing in a dream, that which is performed lacks the characteristic of actual reality.
Likewise, when a person dreams of occupying the highest position, that too lacks the characteristic of being truly superior.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that the luminosity of consciousness destroys the marks of grasping and rejecting.
Since the nature of consciousness is thus, how could external objects exist?
Therefore, all phenomena possess no external referents.

One should know that all forms and appearances manifested by consciousness are the radiance of one's own cognition shining forth as forms and appearances—just as when a person perceives illusions, mirages, or cities of the Gandharvas and grasps them as real.

The way in which ignorant people, with minds of deluded attachment, perceive form and other phenomena as real is likewise like this; it is because of this self-grasping that the mind functions in accordance with them.

As previously explained regarding the meaning of the aggregates, bases, and elements, one should know that apart from those various distinctions of parts, they are merely designated as states of the mind, and thus their manifold characteristics are manifestations of the mind alone.
This meaning is established as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. In this regard, it asks:
"Regarding the five aggregates previously mentioned, what is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of consciousness?
It answers:
As it has been explained regarding the meaning of *citta*, so it is with *vijñāna*.
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has constantly declared:
"One should know that all things are manifested solely by the mind."
This meaning is extremely profound; because those who are ignorant cannot comprehend it, they do not perceive reality.
Therefore, if one can empty the mark of self, one will not give rise to discrimination regarding this mind.
The arising of conceptual discrimination is due to false teachings; therefore, the meaning established by them is not accomplished.

As for the meaning according to reality, one perceives the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), which is the meaning of the selflessness of phenomena within the Mahāyāna. Because one’s own mind is fundamentally non-arising, whatever arises is likewise equal. By means of the sovereign power of one’s own mind, one enters the true meaning, as this is produced through the gateway of yogic practice.
In this regard, it should be understood that the subsequent basis lacks substantial reality; this is precisely what is termed the manifestation of the pure mind.
If a phenomenon belongs to the past, the past has no reality;
if a phenomenon belongs to the future, the future has not yet arrived.
If present phenomena do not abide in the present, how could they abide within the three periods of time?

Just as an army, a forest, and so forth are established through the aggregation of many factors, one should know that consciousness is characterized by selflessness; furthermore, that consciousness does not serve as a substratum.
If one views all phenomena in this way, they will quickly disperse and vanish like a crimson cloud.
Therefore, you should know that if a phenomenon exists, it appears from volition; the ālayavijñāna is likewise so.
The coming and going of all sentient beings is the natural law; it is just as the great ocean is the destination of all streams, so too is the ālayavijñāna the basis for all things.
If one observes that consciousness in such a manner, then no conceptualizing mind can arise.
If each [aspect] is known as it truly is, how then could those various names be spoken?
If each [of these] were to know the nature of all things, they would each be unable to describe them.
This statement is a definitive one; therefore, all phenomena also arise definitively, and they are accomplished in accordance with their functioning across all matters.
The knower and the known constitute a dual distinction; if the known does not exist, how can the knower be established?
Since both are devoid of reality, how can phenomena be attained?

Therefore, one should know that what is called "mind" is merely a name; that name, moreover, cannot be found as something distinct. It exists only for the purpose of signifying, and thus the intrinsic nature of that name is also unattainable.

For this reason, the wise should contemplate that the self-nature of the bodhicitta is like an illusion; whether internally, externally, or in between the two, it cannot be found when sought. There is no dharma to be grasped and no dharma to be abandoned; it is not visible as a shape, nor can it be manifested as a color; it is neither male, female, nor neuter. It does not abide within any form or appearance, and there is no dharma to be seen, for it is not an object of the eye.
Only all Buddhas observe with equanimity whether the nature of the mind has intrinsic nature or lacks intrinsic nature; how could it be seen within the dharma of equality?
That which is called "nature" is merely a designation for conceptual discrimination; if one is free from discrimination, both mind and nature are empty.
If there were a mind that could be perceived through conceptual differentiation, how could it be said therein that it is empty?
Therefore, one should know that there is neither a subject who perceives nor an object that is perceived.
If one can contemplate the bodhicitta in this way, one sees the Tathāgata.

If there were both a subject that awakens and an object to be awakened, the bodhicitta could not be established; therefore, it is signless and unborn, beyond the path of language, and cannot be extolled by words.

Furthermore, the bodhicitta is like space; the mind and space both lack dual characteristics. This explains that the emptiness of the mind and the wisdom of emptiness are equal, and that the supernormal powers of all Buddhas and the nature of all Buddhas are without distinction.

All the activities of all Buddhas throughout the three periods of time are entirely contained and gathered within the realm of bodhi; although all those phenomena are thus contained and gathered, they remain eternally quiescent.

Furthermore, one observes that these impermanent phenomena are like illusions and transformations; they are not to be grasped or stored, for they subdue the three realms of existence by abiding in the dharma of emptiness.

That all things are unarisen is explained as emptiness, and that all things are selfless is also explained as emptiness. If one were to regard this non-arising and selflessness as the observation of emptiness, then that observation would not be established.
The two types of conceptualization—defilement and purity—constitute the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.

If one says that emptiness is observed by means of wisdom, that emptiness likewise has no separate substantial essence; therefore, the bodhicitta is free from all objects of perception and abides in the nature of space.
If one contemplates empty space as that which is dwelt in, there should then be a distinction between the two names "emptiness" and "nature.

Therefore, know that emptiness is like the single roar of a lion in the world, by which all beasts are terrified; it is like a single word of "space," by which all other words are silenced. Thus, know that all places are eternally quiescent and that each and every thing is empty.
Furthermore, the phenomenon of consciousness is an impermanent phenomenon; it arises from the impermanent, and that very nature of impermanence is the bodhicitta.
This explanation does not contradict the meaning of emptiness.

If the nature of impermanence were itself the bodhicitta, then one who delights in bodhi would have a mind that is equanimous; yet, you do not say that they delight in emptiness either. How, then, could a mind that grasps at emptiness be attained?
One should know that the primordial nature of reality is true, and that it encompasses the entire meaning of the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, one should know that phenomena lack intrinsic nature; this absence of intrinsic nature is the meaning of what is here taught.
Regarding what has been said here, as for what this "mind" is:

if it is separated from self and dharmas, the mind does not abide; it is neither a single dharma nor various dharmas, for each possesses its own intrinsic nature, yet that intrinsic nature is itself devoid of self-nature.
Just as worldly molasses has sweetness as its intrinsic nature, and fire has heat as its intrinsic nature, so too is the intrinsic nature of those phenomena emptiness.
That nature of phenomena is neither eternal nor annihilated, neither attained nor abandoned.

For this reason, with ignorance as the beginning and old age and death as the end, all dependently arisen phenomena are established; they are like dreams and illusions, their essence being without reality.

Based on this, they are called the twelve links of existence; these are also termed the wheel of twelve links, which revolves within the gateway of birth and death. Yet, in reality, there is no self and no distinct sentient beings, nor is there any differentiation in the karmic results of the three types of action.

If one understands the phenomena of dependent origination within this, one is able to transcend the gates of all objective spheres; for that is not a mode of conditioned activity, nor does it destroy the correct cause, since it arises from the aggregates.
Because the final limit of saṃsāra is not a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskāra), and because all things arise from the emptiness of emptiness (śūnyatā-śūnyatā) which sustains nothing;
that phenomena are equal in their creation of causes and reception of fruits—this is what the Buddha has taught.

All phenomena arise from the aggregation of various factors; just as there is sound when a drum is struck, or as a sprout grows when barley is sown, so too is the principle of the aggregation of phenomena: they appear through conditions, like illusions or dreams.
All phenomena arise from causes yet are themselves without arising; since their causes are empty of self-nature, what could possibly arise?
Therefore, one should know that all phenomena are unarisen, and this very non-arising is designated as emptiness.
As it is said that the five aggregates are equal in their nature as aggregates, one should likewise contemplate all phenomena in this way.

If one speaks of emptiness as being spoken of in accordance with reality, the essence of that which is spoken of as empty is not annihilation; within this non-annihilated essence, even "reality" is unattainable. To speak of its essence is to call it empty, yet even that emptiness has no essence.
If one realizes that there is no substantial reality, then the agent is impermanent and the body is a collection of various afflictions and karmas; these karmas, in turn, arise from the mind.
If the mind has no abiding, how could karma exist?
Just as a joyful mind is of the nature of tranquility, that tranquil mind cannot be grasped;
those who possess wisdom are able to observe it as it truly is, and by seeing reality, they attain liberation.
Furthermore, the bodhicitta is the supreme reality; this meaning of reality is called emptiness, and it is also called suchness and the limit of reality. This is the signless ultimate truth.

If one does not understand the meaning of emptiness in this way, it should be known that such a person lacks the factors conducive to liberation; they are profoundly deluded within saṃsāra and wander through the six realms as a traveler in cyclic existence.

If there is a wise person who can contemplate that bodhicitta as it truly is—in union with emptiness—and having contemplated thus, is able to accomplish the wisdom of benefiting others, unimpeded and unattached, this person is one who knows gratitude and repays the Buddha’s kindness. Such a person constantly regards all sentient beings with a heart of compassion as their parents and kinsmen, seeing them in their various forms; they perceive how the fierce fires of affliction are constantly burning them, causing all sentient beings to wander in the cycle of birth and death. They resolve to take upon themselves whatever suffering those beings endure, and they resolve to universally bestow upon them whatever happiness they have gathered.

Furthermore, one contemplates how the fruits of the agreeable and disagreeable, the happy and miserable realms, and benefit and harm follow along with sentient beings; yet these sentient beings have originally attained nothing, and various appearances arise according to the distinctions of their wisdom.
All the Brahma kings, Śakras, world-protecting devas, and others—whether gods or humans—are none of them free from worldly characteristics.

Furthermore, he observes all those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals; among these various realms, all sentient beings possess immeasurable and innumerable types of physical forms and appearances. They are constantly pursued by non-beneficial suffering, oppressed by hunger and thirst, and perpetually kill and devour one another. Because of this, they do not escape the fruit of suffering.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to observe, according to reality, the nature of the various karmic retributions of all sentient beings in the happy and miserable realms; having observed them thus, they give rise to the mind of skillful means to well protect sentient beings and cause them to be free from all defilements.

Because all bodhisattvas take great compassion as their fundamental root and take those sentient beings as their objective referent, they do not cling to the savor of any meditative concentration, nor do they seek the karmic rewards obtained through self-benefit. Thus, they transcend the stage of the śrāvakas, do not abandon sentient beings while cultivating practices for the benefit of others, give rise to the great mind of enlightenment, sprout the great shoot of bodhi, and seek the fruit of buddha-enlightenment.

With a heart of great compassion, he observes the suffering of sentient beings: the Avīci Hell is vast and boundless, where beings revolve through karmic retributions according to their various causes of action.
Undergoing all manner of sufferings for these various transgressions, the Bodhisattva, out of his compassionate heart, thinks of taking them upon himself.
These various sufferings possess various characteristics; it is said that they have no reality, yet they are not without reality.
If one thoroughly understands emptiness, one will know that these phenomena proceed accordingly in accordance with the fruits of various karmas.

Therefore, for the sake of rescuing and delivering all sentient beings, the bodhisattvas give rise to a courageous mind and enter the mire of birth and death; though they dwell within birth and death, they remain without defilement or attachment, just as a lotus flower is pure and unstained.

Taking great compassion as its essence, it does not abandon sentient beings; that which is observed by the wisdom of emptiness is not separate from afflictions. Therefore, by the power of skillful means, the Bodhisattva manifests birth in a royal palace, the departure from the city, the practice of asceticism and the cultivation of the Way, sitting at the site of enlightenment to achieve equal and perfect awakening, manifesting supernatural powers to defeat the armies of Māra, turning the Great Wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings, manifesting the three jeweled staircases to descend from heaven and arising in various transformative manifestations, and entering Great Nirvāṇa in accordance with the ways of the world.
Within that interval, he manifests various forms and appearances, appearing sometimes as Brahmā, sometimes as Śakra, or as gods or humans, transforming according to these various characteristics.
By thus manifesting such diverse appearances, he is therefore named the World-Saving Teacher.

All of these are the great compassionate power of the vows of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which subdues the world and causes all beings to dwell securely in corresponding sublime practices; therefore, they do not give rise to weariness or retreat within saṃsāra.
Within the One Vehicle (ekayāna), the teachings of the Two Vehicles (dviyāna) are expounded; thus, both the One Vehicle and the Two Vehicles are of ultimate reality.

Whether it be the enlightenment of a śrāvaka or the enlightenment of a Buddha, the body of wisdom (jñānakāya) is of a single characteristic and samādhi is of a single essence. Although there is that which is spoken, such speech is ultimately non-speech.
As for those who speak of various characteristics, it is merely for the purpose of guiding sentient beings.
If sentient beings attain benefit, the Buddha’s bodhi is equal in merit and wisdom; in reality, there are no two distinct characteristics in which one may abide.
If there were any abiding characteristic, it would constitute a seed; since those seeds aggregate to produce their respective categories, they cause the sprouts and stalks of birth and death to grow.

As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has constantly proclaimed, he destroys the various phenomenal characteristics of the world merely as a skillful means for sentient beings, yet in reality, he does not destroy them.

If one is free from conceptual differentiation, this meaning is profoundly deep; within this profound meaning, there are no two characteristics. Although it is said that there is "destruction," even this is not destruction.
Within the dharma of emptiness, there are no two characteristics; all dharmas maintain their own intrinsic nature as reality.
The perfection of wisdom is itself the bodhicitta, and the bodhicitta eliminates all views.
Therefore, one should know that body, speech, and mind are impermanent phenomena, existing only for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
In this context, that which is called "emptiness" is empty yet not nihilistic;
that which is here spoken of as "existence" exists yet is not eternal.
Therefore, there is neither birth-and-death nor nirvana, and all abide in the non-abiding nirvana.
All the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have declared that the immeasurable mass of merit born of a compassionate heart is itself the supreme, true principle of emptiness;
it is produced by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas and accomplishes the two practices of self-benefit and benefiting others.

I now prostrate to all those natures; I always revere that bodhicitta. May the lineage of Buddhas, which is so highly praised, never be interrupted, and may the World-Honored Buddhas abide forever in the world.
Furthermore, the bodhicitta is the most supreme within the Mahāyāna; I abide in right mindfulness toward this mind.

Moreover, the bodhicitta dwells in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-citta*) and arises from skillful means (*upāya*); if one realizes that this mind is equal to saṃsāra, the two practices of benefiting oneself and benefiting others will be accomplished.
Furthermore, the bodhicitta is free from all marks of views; it proceeds as the reality of non-conceptual wisdom.
Any wise person who generates the bodhicitta shall obtain an immeasurable and boundless accumulation of merit.
Furthermore, if a person contemplates bodhicitta for even a single kṣaṇa, they will obtain an immeasurable mass of merit, because bodhicitta itself is immeasurable.

Furthermore, the jewel of the bodhicitta is pure and unstained; it is the greatest, the most excellent, the supreme, and the foremost. It cannot be destroyed, nor is it subject to destruction; it is true and firm. It can shatter all demons, such as the afflictions, and fulfill all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra for all bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the bodhicitta is the destination to which all phenomena converge.
It is the truth that has been taught, free from all conceptual proliferation; it is the gateway to the pure conduct of Samantabhadra, which is devoid of all marks.
Thus it is said: "The Bodhicitta that I have praised, as correctly taught by the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, is most supreme; the mass of merit obtained from it is likewise immeasurable."
I dedicate this merit to all sentient beings, universally wishing that they may swiftly transcend the ocean of the three realms of existence;
as it has been extolled according to principle and reality, the wise should train themselves in this way.
Treatise on the Non-Conceptual Nature of the Bodhicitta
